381.t: Lucky Millinder's perfect four at a crap game and his spiritualist side
381.s: At a Charleston station Lucky made a hard four first roll on someone else's dice; Francis says he was psychic and worked as Professor Wilson, a spiritualist, in the South.
381.ch: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
381.q: Well, I tell you -- one of the things that used to happen in that band was we used to have a lot of crap games going on, and one night we finished playing in Charleston, South Carolina at the North Station -- I think that's the station in Charleston, waiting for the train to come in.

381.t: Crap games, the Ink Spots package and sandpapered dice
381.s: Hinton and Francis trade stories of constant dice games; Bill Kinney of the Ink Spots kept Francis broke and his sanded dice backfired.
381.ch: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
381.q: No, I don't think so. I think I had the worst luck, because I'll tell you this story. We were traveling with the Ink Spots. The Ink Spots was owned by the same agency that owned Lucky's band, so we used to have a package -- and this package we had, Sister Thorpe, Peg Leg Bates, Timmie and Freddie,…

381.t: The blackjack game that lost his suit money, and the end of his gambling
381.s: Paid at the Adams Theatre in Newark, he dealt blackjack to Lucky and others, lost his pay, and came home to tell his wife there would be no suits.
381.ch: Gambling, Cab's small groups and Havana
381.q: But you know, when we were traveling with the Ink Spots, there were some funny things that used to happen there with the gambling. 112.t: Lost in Atlantic City, gambling with Charlie Johnson
112.s: Out of school and adrift, he gambles with Johnson, whom he calls a great cabaret pianist and bandleader who died poor.
112.q: : Well, no. I'm trying to live there. 'Cause see, I don't want to go back to school, and I don't want to go back to Philadelphia where my people are and all, you see. I'm lost. I don't know what to do. That's right, I'm really lost. I don't know what it's all about. I jumped out of school and…

112.t: Atlantic City 1915 and breaking the gambling habit
112.s: Wooding recalls going to Atlantic City with an entertainer, Charley Johnson teaching him to gamble, and his quitting after a Sunday morning.
112.ch: Charley Johnson and the Army band
112.q: Well, this was around the latter part of 1915. And I was just in the practice of being a pianist. I didn't know how it was going to turn out because I was really lost. I'd dropped out of high school and now I was trying to make it on my own because I was going against the wishes of my parents.

863.t: Audit of the San Jacinto Club's books and the missing money
863.s: As an audit committee member he finds the treasurer borrowed against the club and the books short $2,200; secretary Monette gambled collected money away on a card game.
863.q: And, so, the president told him, he would take and it was going to make him the, the chairman of the, of the board and he had to pick out nine members, besides himself, which would be the, to examine the books. And, uh, we, uh, got together and had a meeting and, and that was the worst night I ever…

83.s: Matassa explains why houses need no cheating, dice chants and the evolution of crooked dice.

194.t: Gambling and card playing after the CCC
194.s: He returned and mostly gambled, explaining Coon Can and calling himself a professional card player; Quint says cards supported him through the 1950s.
194.ch: CCC camp, field work and gambling
194.q: How is it played? Well it's so long. Pity Pat is a short way of pronouncing Coon Camp. The only thing, if you're playing Pity Pat you use one chord against the other. Coon Camp you have to use two against one. To use this one queen you have to have two queens in your hand. Right. So if this is…

323.t: Gambling habit and leaving New Orleans
323.s: He lost money shooting dice and stopped when he left New Orleans on July 3, 1933.
323.q: Yeah I finally got out of it when I left New Orleans to come to New York. Matter of fact I’ll never forget the day. July 3, 1933, Southern Railroad on Canal Street.

1.t: Never gambling; Milt loses at cards in Cab Calloway's band
1.s: Danny lost money shooting dice once and never gambled; Milt recalls losing to Illinois Jacquet and Russell Smith in Cab's band.
1.ch: Becoming a musician: ukulele, clarinet and the Boozaire Kings
1.q: Now, as far as me going through [t'rou] my money, I'd never gamble, because I lost my money once shooting dice with some kids. This little cat could shoot dice, and I didn't know, I just wanted to be a smart-aleck, and he just won my money. I don't know how to shoot dice until today. I never did…

28.t: Losing at dice at the Smart Set Social Club
28.s: Paid five dollars for a gig, he gambled upstairs, lost it, was kicked down the stairs by the caretaker and never gambled again.
28.q: had to forget that. So now I'm playing my gigs and things are running smooth. So they had a little gathering up on the second floor, called the Smart Set Social Club, so I said I'm going up here and try my hand out in the gambling. I went up there and they paid me $5.00 for that gig and I said,…

452.t: Taking cut of the money thrown at T-Bone Walker
452.s: As show director Cobb gathered the money thrown at T-Bone, who gambled it away in crap games, so he pocketed some for himself.
452.q: All right. T-Bone would get on the show and they'd throw all kinds -- twenty-dollar bills, I was pretty honest -- boy from Texas -- on me, and I took up the change and the bills every day and I'd meet him backstage and I was director of the show, and give him all his money; he'd give me ten…

93.t: Galloping dominoes: dice decide the number of steps
93.s: Green describes Robinson's game of galloping dominoes where the roll set the number of tap steps, aiming for eight, which fixed 32-bar choruses.
93.ch: Bill Robinson and Chuck and Chuckles
93.q: Well, he would say words, you know, a way of talking. He would introduce new plays, like in sports. Like who could throw the darts. You know. Who could balance the cards or make a card house, and so forth. Or who could play dice, dominoes, galloping dominoes. That was a pastime.

115.s: Everyone gambled on the bus; he nearly broke Kenny of the Ink Spots in Seattle but lost his nerve.
115.ch: Postwar: Chicago, Vinson, Hines and Cootie
115.q: Well, I got chicken again and wouldn't bet him on that last hand. And I had him beat. Had him beat. I'd have of broke him, too. Sure would have. Gee.
